cookingHelperGuide.title: Comprehensive Cooking Science & Techniques Helper
cookingHelperGuide.description: Integrated knowledge from multiple cookbooks with food science principles, cooking tips, fermentation science, and AI-powered recipe assistance
sources: The Art of Fermentation - Sandor Ellix Katz
Mastering the Art of Soviet Cooking - Anya Von Bremzen
The Designers Dictionary of Color - Sean Adams (color in food)

ingredientSelection.tip: When shopping for dried chiles, give them a little squeeze through the bag—if they feel brittle, they're likely old and won't have great flavor. Look for dried chiles that have a nice, deep color and are still a little soft.

Stock essential dry goods that are shelf-stable: piloncillo sugar, Mexican vanilla, Ceylon cinnamon (milder than cassia), dried Mexican oregano, dried beans, tomato sauce, and good olive oil. A well-stocked pantry means you can throw together something delicious with whatever else you have in the fridge.
Always keep fresh lemons and limes on hand. Store cilantro like a bouquet of flowers in a jar of water in the fridge—it will keep longer and add fragrance to your kitchen.

Use Diamond Crystal kosher salt for recipes calling for precise measurements. If using Morton kosher, reduce the quantity by half due to density differences. For finishing, use flaky salt for better texture and visual appeal.

cookingTechniques.description: Olive oil has a slightly lower smoke point than some other vegetable oils
cookingTechniques.rule: Keep oil temperature under 400°F when frying. Use regular olive oil for frying, not extra-virgin.
cookingTechniques.why: Extra-virgin olive oil has a lower smoke point (~375°F) while regular olive oil can handle ~400°F

cookingTechniques.description: Corn flour for tortillas and masa-based dishes
cookingTechniques.rule: Use nixtamalized masa harina (check the bag). Maseca is common, but Masienda makes excellent heirloom corn versions.
cookingTechniques.why: Nixtamalization process makes corn more nutritious and flavorful

cookingTechniques.description: Low and slow cooking method for meat dishes and beans
cookingTechniques.rule: Perfect for: Chicken Tinga, Pork Ribs, Beans - develops deep flavors through extended cooking
cookingTechniques.why: Low heat breaks down connective tissue and develops complex flavors

cookingTechniques.rule: Comals were used in Mesoamerican kitchens, made from clay (traditional) or cast iron (modern). Can substitute well-seasoned cast iron or large nonstick skillet.
cookingTechniques.why: Flat surface allows even heat distribution for tortillas and griddle cooking

substitutions.note: Piloncillo is slightly sweeter and more caramel-y, but brown sugar works well
Mexican vanilla is more aromatic; 80% of vanilla now comes from Madagascar
Ceylon is milder and more delicate; cassia is stronger
Mexican oregano is actually verbena family, brighter and more citrus-y

substitutions.ratio: 1 can = 1 can diced tomatoes + 1 diced jalapeño
substitutions.note: Ro-Tel is a Tex-Mex staple; adds spicy flavor

chemicalReactions.description: Microorganisms break down organic compounds in the absence of oxygen
chemicalReactions.equation: Glucose → Lactic Acid + Ethanol + CO2 (depending on type)
chemicalReactions.timeframe: Hours to months depending on conditions

chemicalReactions.description: Lactobacillus bacteria convert sugars to lactic acid

conditions.salinity: 2-5% salt creates environment favorable for lactobacillus
conditions.pH: Starts neutral, drops to 3.5-4.5 as acid develops

chemicalReactions.duration: 3 days to 3 months depending on temperature and taste preference

chemicalReactions.description: As fermentation progresses, complex compounds develop

chapters.title: Acetic Acid Fermentation

chemicalReactions.description: Acetobacter bacteria oxidize ethanol to acetic acid

requirements.substrate: Started from wine, cider, or other fermented liquid

chemicalReactions.description: Mother culture and aging create depth
chemicalReactions.notes: The 'mother' is living culture of acetobacter that can ferment new batches
chemicalReactions.aging: Wooden barrel aging adds tannins and complexity

applications: Kombucha (dual fermentation: sugar + tannins with SCOBY)

chapters.title: Alcoholic Fermentation

chemicalReactions.description: Saccharomyces cerevisiae converts sugars to ethanol and CO2

conditions.temperature: 60-75°F for ale yeasts, 50-55°F for lager yeasts
conditions.sugar_source: Glucose, fructose, or other simple sugars
conditions.duration: 1-4 weeks depending on yeast and conditions

products: Ethanol (2-15% depending on yeast strain and sugar)

chemicalReactions.description: Yeast produces esters and other compounds
factors: Oxygen availability (initial fermentation needs some O2)

chemistry: Yeast metabolism creates hundreds of flavor compounds
Different yeast strains produce different flavor profiles
Temperature control is critical for flavor development
Aging allows esters to develop and harsh notes to mellow

chapters.title: Koji Fermentation & Mold Culture

enzymes: Protease - breaks proteins into amino acids
Lipase - breaks fats into fatty acids
chemicalReactions.application: Converts complex compounds into simpler, more flavorful and digestible forms

chemicalReactions.description: White mold colonizes grain or beans

umami: Koji enzymes break proteins into free amino acids
Forms basis for miso, soy sauce, other umami foods

chapters.title: Multiple Simultaneous Fermentations

chemicalReactions.description: Multiple microbes working together create complex flavors
organisms: Acetobacter (bacteria) - converts ethanol to acetic acid
sequence: Initial fermentation: Yeast consumes sugar, produces ethanol
Secondary fermentation: Bacteria oxidize ethanol to acetic acid
Final product: Slightly alcoholic, slightly sour, complex flavored beverage

chemicalReactions.results: Unique, complex flavor profiles from local microbes

applications: Complex vegetable ferments with multiple ingredients

commonIssues.problem: White mold or film on surface
commonIssues.cause: Kahm yeast or wild mold contamination
commonIssues.solution: Skim off; ferment is usually still safe if no smell

commonIssues.cause: Excess moisture, improper salt ratio, wrong temperature
commonIssues.prevention: Use 2-5% salt, maintain 60-75°F, ensure anaerobic conditions
commonIssues.solution: Check salt ratio, improve aeration control

commonIssues.cause: Temperature too cold, insufficient salt, wrong substrate
commonIssues.prevention: Maintain proper temperature, use fresh vegetables with natural bacteria
commonIssues.solution: Warm environment, add quality salt, check vegetable freshness

commonIssues.prevention: Sanitize equipment, use proper salt and water ratios
commonIssues.solution: Start fresh batch with better conditions

colorInCooking.title: The Role of Color in Food & Visual Appetizing
colorInCooking.principle: Food appearance affects flavor perception and appetite

concepts.description: Colors trigger psychological and appetite responses
examples: Red/Orange - warmth, appetite stimulation (tomatoes, peppers, spices)
Golden brown - richness, depth, Maillard reaction success
Dark brown/black - intensity, sophistication (dark chocolate, soy sauce)

concepts.description: Visual balance makes food more appealing
techniques: Pair complementary colors (red tomatoes + green basil + white cream)
Garnish with herbs for color pop

concepts.description: Color signals food quality and freshness
indicators: Pale color = undercooked or poor preparation

features.description: Users upload photos of their cooking progress for real-time feedback
capabilities: Identify cooking stage (raw, seared, fully cooked, etc.)
Identify color indicators (golden, charred, pale, etc.)
Recognize common issues (sticking, burning, curdling, etc.)

features.description: AI provides specific guidance based on current step
analysis: Compare image to expected appearance at this step
Provide encouragement or caution as needed

features.description: System learns from user images and feedback
training: Model learns what different doneness levels look like
Builds personalized understanding of user's cooking style

issues: Sticking/burning - suggest lower heat or more oil
Overcooked - suggest ending early next time
Not browning properly - suggest higher heat or longer sear
Sauce breaking/curdling - suggest lower temp or slower additions
Meat/fish not resting - suggest timing adjustments
Vegetables not tender - suggest different prep or timing

uploadInterface.description: User-friendly image upload for each recipe step
uploadInterface.feedback: AI responds within 5 seconds with analysis and suggestions

questions: Did the AI correctly identify the doneness?
Is your result similar to the photo or different?
What adjustment would have been better?
trainingFeedback.learning: Model adjusts weights based on feedback to improve accuracy

whenToUseSlowCooker: Tough cuts of meat that benefit from long, moist cooking
Stews and braises where flavors develop over hours
Beans and legumes for even cooking
Avoid: Quick sears, delicate fish, green vegetables
flavorLayering: Start with aromatics (onion, garlic) in oil to build base
Add proteins and vegetables in order of cooking time
Incorporate spices early to toast and bloom them
Add herbs in two stages: hardy herbs early, delicate herbs at end
Finish with acid (citrus, vinegar) to brighten final flavor
temperatureControl: Low and slow (200-250°F): Breaking down collagen, developing umami
Very high (500°F+): Searing, charring (briefly to prevent burning)
